definition: A company (e.g. Broadcom, Marvell, MediaTek, Alchip, GUC) that turns a customer's chip architecture into manufacturable silicon, supplying physical design, high-speed SerDes, packaging and foundry access. Hyperscalers use them to build custom accelerators without hiring a full chip team.

Designing chips together with the compilers, libraries and models that run on them, so a new feature such as an FP4 number format is usable on launch day. NVIDIA's main silicon advantage in 2026 is co-design speed rather than raw specifications.

Software used to design and verify chips, from logic synthesis to physical layout and sign-off; Synopsys and Cadence dominate. Every new chip program pays EDA licences, and NVIDIA holds a $2B Synopsys stake.
Part of an acquisition price paid later only if the acquired business hits agreed milestones, such as revenue targets. Used to bridge valuation gaps, e.g. in Marvell's purchase of Celestial AI.
Revenue minus cost of goods sold, as a share of revenue. NVIDIA's GAAP gross margin was about 75% in mid-2026; the chip-only margin on a GPU is estimated nearer 80%.
One of the largest cloud operators (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, Oracle) that buy accelerators by the hundreds of thousands and increasingly design their own chips.

Groq's inference accelerator design that keeps model weights in on-chip SRAM and schedules every operation at compile time, trading memory capacity for very fast token generation. NVIDIA licensed it in 2025 and ships it as the Groq 3 LPU.
Chips sold on the open market to any buyer (NVIDIA GPUs, AMD Instinct), as opposed to custom chips a company designs for its own use (Google TPU, AWS Trainium).

Placing compute logic inside or right next to memory so data travels a shorter distance, raising effective bandwidth and cutting energy per operation; Qualcomm's AI250 and d-Matrix use variants of the idea.
The one-time cost of designing a chip, including engineering time, EDA tools, IP licences and photomasks, before any unit is sold. Estimates for a large leading-edge chip run to roughly $0.5-0.7B.
Useful work per unit of power, e.g. FP8 TFLOPS per watt or tokens per second per megawatt. In power-capped data centers it decides how much a site can sell.
The moment a finished chip design is handed to the foundry to make photomasks and first wafers. A failed tape-out costs months and tens of millions of dollars in masks.

A processor built from an entire silicon wafer rather than a single die, as in Cerebras' WSE-3 (46,225 mm², 44 GB of on-chip SRAM). It avoids chip-to-chip links but needs special packaging, power and cooling.
Industry shorthand for a custom AI accelerator designed by or for one customer, such as Google's TPU, AWS Trainium, Microsoft Maia or Meta MTIA.
